issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette:
Carlos was a 65-year-old dentist when a lone gunman opened fire on a crowded cultural fair in his city. He had been walking with his wife, who was killed beside him. He survived physically, but the memory of that afternoon never settled-it returned as a complete sensory reliving, overwhelming him with the same sounds, smells, and terror every time. He could not put it into words; the experience was too raw, too wordless, too much to hold in language.

In the months after, he began to notice changes. A car backfiring on the street would stop him cold-the gunshot noise alone could send him into a full recall of the attack, his heart racing, the scene flooding back as if he were still there. He became hyperalert to unexpected sounds and started watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him. Whenever he entered a room or building, he automatically scanned for exits. At work in his dental practice, a patient's mention of military service or a uniformed officer stopping for a routine check made his chest tighten-authority figures in uniform were now potent triggers.

He came to believe he had failed at the fair, that he should have seen it coming or shielded his wife. This self-blame became a recurring rumination, each cycle of guilt pulling him back into the memory of the event, the sights and sounds returning with fresh intensity. To feel safer, he began carrying a concealed handgun. The weight of the weapon in his jacket pocket was a constant reminder of vulnerability-it also made him more sensitive to any sound that could be a gunshot, and he found himself avoiding news reports about similar attacks because they brought the memory roaring back.

His hypervigilance to threatening sounds kept him on edge, which reinforced his urge to carry the weapon and to avoid military topics or news. The avoidance, in turn, removed any chance to habituate to the triggers, so a single unexpected noise remained capable of triggering a full sensory flashback. And the flashbacks, overwhelming as they were, made him even more watchful of others and more likely to scan exits before he could settle. His rumination about blame made the memory more vivid, and the vivid memory made him more sensitive to any potential trigger-a cycle he could not break.

Carlos retired from dentistry last year, partly because the clinical environment-the drills, the sudden sounds, the anxious patients-had become a landscape of triggers. He still carries the handgun everywhere, and his children have expressed concern. He rarely visits them because their neighborhood is near a military base, and conversations about deployment are too jarring. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at a grocery store: a uniformed security guard startled him, his hand went to his pocket, and he realized he had reached for his gun in public. He is afraid of what he might do, and more afraid of what he might feel if he lets the memory surface without his avoidance.
